new_statements.quote: The speaker should remember that in some compound words the last syllable of the first word, if it end in a, is pronounced strong; e.g.— Patunga-poaka, place where pigs are killed; Mahinga-kai, a cultivation; Mata-pu, the lead of a gun, a bullet; Ta te tutua tu, the plebeian's manners. (p. 2) || First, as it is in English, every sentence is to be pronounced as if one word. (p. 7) || The speaker should be always careful, in pronouncing the passive a, to throw the emphasis strongly on the last syllable. The following words are of this description:— Panga, to throw away; pana, to shove away, &c.; kanga, to curse; wakamana, to ratify, &c.; taunaha, to bespeak; unga, to send; waha, to carry on the back. (p. 45)

Maunsell adds compatible partial detail only: final-stressed passives in -ā and stressed compound-linking -ā are exactly what the modern weight-sensitive rule (long vowel > diphthong > first syllable, within four morae of the word end; Keegan 2023 citing Harlow 2015, Schütz 1985 quoting Biggs 1969 and Hohepa 1967, Culhane 2024, all already saved in the same check folder) predicts. He never states a general placement rule and never claims initial stress. The Glottolog citation (W. C. Wilson) does not match the archive.org copy (Upton & Co., 4th ed.,…
new_statements.rule_in_words: No general rule for the placement of word stress is stated anywhere in the grammar; the nine-page pronunciation chapter treats vowel qualities, diphthongs and consonants only, and the single occurrence of the word 'accent' (p. 7) merely says that whether a doubtful vowel sequence counts as a diphthong may depend on 'the influence of the accent'. Three partial observations are usable: (a) in some compounds the final syllable of the first member is 'pronounced strong' when it ends in a (Patunga-poaka, Mahinga-kai, Mata-pu), with exceptions; (b) the passive suffix -a (modern -ā: pangā, panā, kangā, whakamanā, taunahā, ungā, wahā) takes strong 'emphasis' on the final syllable, i.e. such passives are final-stressed; (c) a whole sentence is pronounced as one word (phrase-level phonology). Maunsell does not mark vowel length and describes it impressionistically (three 'sounds' of a; long and short o; quick and slow u), so his 'strong'/'emphasis' remarks are the 19th-century way of registering the modern observation that long vowels attract stress.
new_statements.exceptions: On the compound rule (p. 2): 'Note.—There are exceptions to this rule which it would be well for the student of observation to notice.' On the passive: 'On the Eastern Coast ia takes the place of simple a in the passive; e.g. maka, makaia' (p. 45), i.e. the final-emphasis passives in -a are the western (Waikato) forms.
new_statements.identity_note: Maunsell wrote at Waikato Heads (preface dated February 1842) and says the Waikato dialect 'is very generally known throughout the larger portion of the island'; the grammar describes New Zealand Maori generally with dialect notes (Ngapuhi, Waikato, Rotorua, Bay of Plenty, East Coast, Taranaki; a dialect table on p. 9). The passive-emphasis remark applies to the western -a passives, with the note that the East Coast uses -ia instead.

audit.recode_to: kind: unchanged (weight-hedged, weight-sensitive (tentative); heavy = CV: and CVV, CV: outranks CVV). edge: 'unbounded' -> 'right' with a four-mora right-edge window in the primary-stress rule (catalog convention as in mana1295/nepa1254): 'main stress may not fall more than four morae (vowels) from the end of the word; inside that window stress the first long vowel, else the first diphthong (for some speakers any non-final diphthong), else the first syllable of the window' (Biggs 1969:132-3 rules 1-3,5 as quoted verbatim in Schutz 1985:9; Biggs 1978:700 'among the final four, which is as far forward as phrase-stress may move'; Harlow 2007:82 and Bauer 1993:546-7 as relayed by Culhane 2024:1070 and Thompson et al. 2011:1983; Mixdorff et al. 2018:631; Keegan 2023). Biggs' own examples show the window overriding 'leftmost long vowel' in words >4 morae: aanIwaniwa, kaarAmuramu, PaarEmoremo, haaEreere carry heaviest stress on the fourth vowel from the end, not on the initial long vowel (Biggs 1969:133 rule 4, in Schutz 1985:9). quote/cite: replace the StressTyp2-carried Hyman 1977:51 tail with its primary, Hohepa 1967:10, verbatim in Schutz 1985:8: 'stem stress is predictable.. Major stress will fall on the first syllable containing a geminate cluster, if none, then on the first syllable with a non-identical vowel cluster, and if none, then on the first syllable. Secondary stress will fall on the subsequent syllable which fills the highest order of precedence after the major stress..'. domain/hedge note: Biggs 1978:699 'the fact that single words said alone are final phrases, and stressed accordingly, has given rise to the belief that Maori has word-initial stress. However, in non-final phrases any appropriately-placed word takes phrase-stress on the penultimate syllable'; Schutz 1985:22-23 'Accent in Maori cannot be described as either phonemic or predictable'; keep weight-sensitive (tentative).
